clue.text: She foiled Haman, immersing his head in a chemical compound

indicators.note: the compound is said to immerse, so it surrounds the other letter

parts.note: an ester is an organic compound formed from an acid and an alcohol

indicators.note: the head of the word his is its first letter

explanation.surface: A biblical heroine defeats her enemy by dunking his head in a chemical bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'immersing' puts H, the head of 'his', inside ESTER.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Esther the Jewish queen exposed and thwarted the plotting minister Haman.

clue.text: But the continental one is no supporter of 13s

definitions.text: But the continental one is no supporter of 13s

parts.words: But the continental one is no supporter of 13s
parts.note: 13 across is a volume one might reserve; furniture holding volumes contrasts with the undersea ledge fringing a continent

explanation.surface: A remark that one European kind does not support certain volumes.
explanation.walkthrough: The continental kind is the submerged ledge around a landmass, which holds up no books.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledge holds volumes; the continental one is the shallow seabed around a continent.

clue.text: Such a one does not rule the roost

definitions.text: Such a one does not rule the roost

parts.words: Such a one does not rule the roost
parts.note: ruling the roost is being boss at home; this husband is dominated by a nagging wife, like a cockerel bullied by hens

explanation.definitionFit: A husband who is nagged and bossed by his wife is far from master of the household.

clue.text: Three men in this boat raced with eg Chaucer

parts.note: ran is the past tense of run, so raced
Dan, meaning master, is the old honorific in 'Dan Chaucer', Spenser's name for the poet

explanation.surface: An echo of Three Men in a Boat, racing alongside Chaucer.
explanation.walkthrough: A randan is a rowing boat for three, with the middle rower pulling a pair of sculls.
explanation.definitionFit: This rowing craft is built to be pulled by a crew of three.

clue.text: A bull perhaps, or a Greek at Troy?

explanation.surface: Is a stock-market bull a kind of Greek warrior besieging Troy?
explanation.walkthrough: To invest a city is an old word for to besiege it, so any Greek encamped round Troy was one who invested it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull is a stock-market speculator putting money in; a besieger of Troy was one who 'invested' (surrounded) the city.

clue.text: Musical title Len changed to "The Doctrine of Reason "

indicators.note: the words are changed into a different letter order

explanation.surface: A musical's title is altered by Len to a philosophical name.
explanation.walkthrough: The fifteen letters of MUSICAL, TITLE and LEN are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Rationalism, the belief that knowledge comes from thinking rather than the senses, goes by this name.

clue.text: Sour-tempered like Joe when pickled ?

explanation.surface: Someone as crabby as a certain Joe, especially when drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vinegar Joe' was the nickname of the irascible US General Joseph Stilwell; 'pickled' then means steeped in vinegar, not drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid in temper, like General Stilwell's nickname; and tasting of the preserving liquid used for pickles.

clue.text: Islam's broken dish

indicators.note: broken means the letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: the possessive 's gives no letter

explanation.surface: A remark that the faith is shattered, or a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges ISLAM.
explanation.definitionFit: A salmi is a ragout of game birds, a classic French stew.

clue.text: Fully extended by an alfresco feast?

parts.note: alfresco means in the open air, outside
a spread is a lavish meal laid out

explanation.surface: Is a picnic feast stretched out to the full?
explanation.definitionFit: Spread wide open, as wings or arms stretched to their full span.

clue.text: Where cricketers compete in knowing fashion

parts.note: kenning, from Scots ken, means knowing
ton is an old word for fashion or high style

explanation.surface: A place where cricketers play in an artful, knowing manner.
explanation.walkthrough: KENNINGTON is the London district where the Oval cricket ground stands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oval, a Test match cricket venue, is in the London district of this name.

clue.text: A rift in it plugged with this clay?

explanation.surface: A crack in something is sealed with this clay.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson wrote of 'the little rift within the lute' that silences the music; the same word names a clay paste used to seal joints.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical instrument is the one with Tennyson's famous rift; the homonym is a sealing cement of clay.

clue.text: Nevertheless where the Duke of Plaza-Toro stationed himself in battle

definitions.text: where the Duke of Plaza-Toro stationed himself in battle

explanation.surface: The comic Gilbert and Sullivan Duke positions himself, in battle, at the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers the Duke of Plaza-Toro 'led his regiment from behind', so he came last of all.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means 'even so'; read literally it puts the cowardly Duke behind everybody else.

clue.text: Almost in the clutch of flu

indicators.note: almost means the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: to be in the clutch of something is to be gripped by it

explanation.surface: Someone nearly in the grip of influenza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' drops the last letter, D, from GRIPPED.
explanation.definitionFit: Grippe is the French-derived term for influenza.

clue.text: It could be an annual reserve

explanation.surface: Something published yearly might also be held back for later.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual is a yearly volume; to reserve a table or seat is to make a booking.

clue.text: Chess played (and Captain Hook got the boot) here

definitions.text: Chess played (and Captain Hook got the boot) here

parts.words: Chess played (and Captain Hook got the boot) here
parts.note: a chess game is played over a chequered board, and Peter Pan's villain was kicked off his ship into the sea

explanation.definitionFit: Over the board is where chess happens; a sailor thrown off a ship goes into the sea this way.

clue.text: Cheer'd in excitement, having won the, pools

indicators.note: the excitement stirs up the letters before it into a new order

parts.note: the clipped form keeps its letters, the apostrophe giving none

explanation.surface: A punter cheers excitedly on winning the football pools.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of CHEERD and IN are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A pools winner has suddenly become wealthy, made rich.

clue.text: Phony type of fish South African province put up

parts.note: char is a fish of the trout family

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting up reverses the province's letters

parts.note: Natal was a province of South Africa

explanation.surface: A fake fish from a South African province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' turns NATAL into LATAN in a down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A quack or impostor who falsely claims skill or knowledge.

clue.text: Does he have always to tear round his parish ?

definitions.text: Does he have always to tear round his parish ?

indicators.note: round means the word for tear goes round the other piece

parts.note: to rend is to tear
ever means always, as in 'for ever'

explanation.surface: A clergyman wonders whether he must always rush around his parish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts EVER inside REND, between its R and END; the whole clue describes a busy vicar.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicar or rector, given this title, has a parish to look after.

clue.text: No quick qualifying race-result inconclusive

parts.note: quick in its old sense is alive, so not quick is lifeless
a heat is a preliminary race deciding who goes through

explanation.surface: A slow qualifying race ends without a clear result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' is the old word for alive, as in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: A race where two finish exactly level has no winner, so its outcome is undecided.

clue.text: A princess of Savoy or Ethiopia

definitions.text: A princess of Savoy or Ethiopia

parts.note: Princess Ida is the heroine of a Gilbert and Sullivan Savoy opera

explanation.surface: A royal heroine from either a Savoy opera or Ethiopia.
explanation.walkthrough: The Savoy operas are Gilbert and Sullivan's; the whole clue also describes Verdi's opera heroine, an Ethiopian princess.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Verdi's opera is an Ethiopian princess held captive in Egypt.

clue.text: Sanctuary — with a Scottish smoker outside its limits

definitions.text: Sanctuary — with a Scottish smoker outside its limits

indicators.note: outside means the other pieces sit around the limits

parts.note: a lum is Scots for a chimney

indicators.note: its limits are the first and last letters of the clue's first word

explanation.surface: A refuge with a Scottish chimney standing outside its boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its limits' points back to the first and last letters of 'Sanctuary', S and Y; 'outside' puts A and LUM around them.
explanation.definitionFit: An asylum is a place of refuge or protection, as in political asylum.

clue.text: Monastic type died recently

parts.note: ob., from Latin obiit, is the abbreviation for died
late can mean recently, as in 'of late'

explanation.surface: A monk passed away not long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblate is a lay person dedicated to a religious community, living by its rule.

clue.text: Fiancée of a Buckingham Palace guardsman

definitions.text: Fiancée of a Buckingham Palace guardsman

parts.words: Fiancée of a Buckingham Palace guardsman
parts.note: in A. A. Milne's poem about changing guard, Christopher Robin's companion is marrying one of the guard

explanation.definitionFit: Milne's poem says this nanny 'is marrying one of the guard'.

clue.text: Ensign Beverley's complete name

explanation.surface: The full name of an army ensign called Beverley.
explanation.walkthrough: In Sheridan's play The Rivals, Captain Jack Absolute woos Lydia disguised as the penniless Ensign Beverley, so that is the Ensign's real surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The disguised suitor in The Rivals bears this surname; the adjective also means total, utter.

clue.text: One asking for more tobacco perhaps

explanation.surface: A person wanting extra tobacco, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's Oliver Twist famously asks the workhouse master for more gruel; twist is also tobacco in a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's orphan holds out his bowl for a second helping; the word also names tobacco wound into a rope.

clue.text: Finish of 24 — a team is hailed in the street

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the solution to 24 down
XI, eleven in Roman numerals, is a cricket or football team

explanation.surface: The end of a match, and a team flags something down in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finish of' takes T, the last letter of TWIST, the answer to 24 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A cab is the vehicle one hails at the kerb.

clue.text: Pilot gets one wrong somewhat. down in the mouth

indicators.note: the letters are put together wrong, so they need rearranging

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A pilot gets something wrong and feels rather glum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down in the mouth' looks like gloom, but it is a location: a little way down the throat.
explanation.definitionFit: This flap of cartilage sits at the back of the throat, a little below the mouth, closing the windpipe when swallowing.

clue.text: Notice Crazy Edmund's rider

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, is a notice

indicators.note: crazy says the letters of the name go haywire

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: An announcement that a man named Edmund has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crazy' rearranges EDMUND into DENDUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider is a clause added to a document, an appendix or supplement.

clue.text: Very little time

explanation.surface: Hardly any time at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronounced one way it means tiny; the other way it is sixty seconds.
